extracted.intended_audience: general NPR/news audience and people interested in journalism/media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practices for producing and vetting a long-form radio/podcast journalism piece (fact-checking, source verification, editorial decisions, and corrections). Focuses on how a public-radio program should evaluate and handle reporting that may include first-person theatrical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to journalistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our program adheres to the same journalistic standards as the other national shows, and in this case, we did not live up to those standards."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program-level obligation to follow established journalism standards for verification, sourcing, and transparency when presenting material as journalism. If standards are not met, the program must acknowledge the failure publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-check many claims; verify key assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: This American Life "says they did fact check many of the claims made about Apple in the piece. But they failed to check out one big one."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform thorough fact-checking of both peripheral and central claims; ensure that the core, potentially explosive assertions are independently verified rather than relying solely on the contributor's word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify source identity and contactability
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass says Daisey lied to him and his producer about the name of his interpreter and he also said the cell phone number he had for her didn't work anymore and he had no way to get back in touch with her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the real name, role, and reliable contact information for key sources and intermediaries; inability to recontact or independently confirm a source should raise red flags for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroborate eyewitness accounts and specific details (locations, numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the falsehoods found in Daisey's monologue are small ones: the number of factories Daisey visited in China, for instance, and the number of workers he spoke with. Others are large. ... he claims to have met a group of workers who were poisoned on an iPhone assembly line by a chemical called n-hexane. Apple's audits ... show that an incident like this occurred in a factory in China, but the factory wasn't located in Shenzhen, where Daisey visited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independently verify specifics such as locations, dates, counts, and chain-of-events; even if similar incidents have occurred elsewhere, confirm that the contributor actually witnessed the particular instance they describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish theater/first-person performance from journalism and label appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Daisey: 'My mistake, the mistake I truly regret, is that I had it on your show as journalism, and it's not journalism. It's theater.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If material is theatrical, subjective, or constructed for effect, it must not be presented as factual reporting. Clearly label performance pieces and avoid excerpting them as journalism without additional verification and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kill the story when key verification is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: "At that point, we should've killed the story," said Glass in a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If editors cannot corroborate essential elements or recontact sources after reasonable effort, the appropriate editorial action is to withhold or delay publication rather than proceed with unverified claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the severity of falsehoods (small vs large) and their editorial impact
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some of the falsehoods found in Daisey's monologue are small ones... Others are large."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between minor inaccuracies (e.g., numerical exaggerations) and substantive fabrications (e.g., invented events or mislocated incidents); treat larger fabrications as more serious breaches requiring corrections, retractions, and review of editorial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external audits and official documents to corroborate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple's audits of its suppliers show that an incident like this occurred in a factory in China, but the factory wasn't located in Shenzhen...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult corporate audits, official reports, and other documentary evidence to corroborate or refute claims, and check whether such documents match the contributor's assertions in place and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be responsive to other outlets' investigative findings and follow up
rubrics_metrics.description: This American Life first learned Daisey had fabricated parts of his story when another public radio program Marketplace tracked down Daisey's interpreter, who disputed parts of Daisey's monologue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When peers or other journalists surface contradictions or new evidence, promptly investigate and, if necessary, update editorial judgments and publicly correct the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue corrections, append notes, and devote coverage to addressing errors
rubrics_metrics.description: For the record, we pointed to the piece in question in a blog post in February. We'll append a note. Also, This American Life will devote a considerable amount of time on Sunday's show to this matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When errors or fabrications are discovered, be transparent: append clear correction notices, run on-air explanations or follow-up coverage, and explain how the failure occurred and what measures will prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider public impact and downstream consequences of airing unverified allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece essentially made Daisey Apple's chief critic and it also inspired a Change.org petition that collected more than 250,000 signatures demanding that Apple better the working conditions at the factories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how broadcasting unverified or dramatized accounts may mobilize public opinion, advocacy, or reputational harm; weigh potential societal consequences when making editorial decisions about airing contested material.
